en: Title: Jātakastava Author: Jñānayaśas Source: Shackleton Bailey 1954; input by Klaus Wille on GRETIL

Tibetan: O Lord, where is this Ten-Powered One, untainted by flaws in his qualities and sovereign in his conduct? And where is my mind, dull as it is regarding the descent and turning back from birth? Yet, because of that very mind, the dust I have cast upon you results in the arising of fruitful rewards; thus, my speech adopts a loquaciousness through its persistence in praising you. Sanskrit: kvedaṃ daśabalaṃ guṇairaśabalaṃ caryāvibhutvaṃ vibho janmasyandanikāvivartanajaḍaṃ cetaḥ kva cedaṃ mama | yenāvandhyaphalodayās tvayi bhavanty abhyāhitāḥ pāṃsavaḥ tena stutyanubandhinā mukharatām ālambate bhāratī || Js_1 ||

The unique virtues of those who have transcended the objects of the mind and possess the vision of tranquility do not fully enter the range of speech; for they are subtle, yet they become manifest even in part to those like me. Indeed, who among seekers can grasp the jewels of the ocean that appear upon the sandy shores near the water—jewels whose luster is like the moonlight shimmering within the breaking waves?

O Victor, that continuum of yours, which was intent on deeds great in following the path to enlightenment and which overflowed with the compassion of a Conqueror for the arising of the world's welfare— [Note: The provided text contains a fragment of verse 2 and the beginning of verse 3. The translation reflects this structure.]

O Blessed One, even now, when your virtues—which have been accumulated over many eons and which spread through the full experience of all that is to be known—are being proclaimed, they purify [the world]; how much more so, then, were those virtues already free from stain for the sake of awakening?
Beholding the unrestrained and intoxicating conduct of the wild elephant of passion, you directed your thoughts toward awakening without ever transgressing your vow;

thus, as if installing the gods themselves in you, they long bestowed upon you the glory of the consecration of Dharma. Therefore, the gods from heaven offered a floral tribute until the tips of the filaments trembled.

Seeing a tigress dwelling within the depths of a mountain cave, her belly exhausted by the pain of hunger and solely intent on devouring her own cubs, you—your mind permeated with compassion—cast off your body clad in bark garments and bearing matted locks; by that act, you became the refuge for embodied beings who must turn away from the abysses of the mountain of worldly existence. And when, assuming the state of an elephant white as a mountain of snow, you were wandering in the midst of a forest to prevent the calamities of living beings, [you acted thus].
By you, who moved the great mountain of massive rocks, your very self was offered; I believe that by this act, the utterly dark dispositions of the envious were destroyed.

Since you, with a body like the moon—the moon of the world’s sky—assumed the state of Candraprabha and gave your head, with its variegated hair-tuft, to a Brahmin who asked for it, shining with the luster of a crest-jewel, your head was severed like a lotus plucked from its stalk with a sword; by that, you have become the preceptor of these worlds, like an *uṣṇīṣa* upon their heads.

O Jina, because you gave away your sons— whose bodies were as tender as young lotuses— to a petitioner, and your wives who followed your will, their eyes rolling and their tufts of hair trembling, the faces of the daughters of Māra surely became sluggish with shame, their petal-like eyelashes drooping in contraction. Formerly, having become a bird wandering through the forest lands during sleep and dreams, you shattered all fragments of this world with your unerring voice, proclaiming the path of the Supreme.

O Lord, because you caused the Kāpiñjala vow—which was practiced by those who bear vows—to reach such great expansion, the shadows cast by the rays of your crown have become the refuge for those afflicted by the disease of ignorance.

O Lord, in former times, while assuming the form of a hare and eating only leaves, water, and fruit, you displayed hospitality out of your long-standing practice of compassion toward a guest who arrived at that moment;
it is for this reason that even now, on earth, the mark upon the orb of the moon is perceived as a hare consisting of your own fame, amidst the clearly visible sparks of fire.

I believe that when the elephant of the God of Love, his eyes red with rage, drew a frown across his brows and brandished his flashing sword, he was unable—even for a moment—to bring himself to strike you, whose mind remained unscarred; for that reason, I think the unrestrained arrows of Smara have met with a fracture at their very feathers. Since you, who possess six tusks, have long worshipped with your tusks the enemy of the elephant [Śiva], who holds a drawn bow and possesses the luster of a mass of white, towering, great clouds.

Even today, in the netherworld (pātāla), the serpents— with their hoods slackened by the terror of your arms, which are cruel with the blood-stained dust vomited from the extraction of their own bellies— still worship you with their fangs. Because you, by means of the great raft of your body, out of love brought to the shore those men whose ships were overturned by the ocean— the lord of waters, terrifying with its garland of waves and agitated by the swarms of sea-monsters (makara) due to the violent tossing of the snakes' hoods— by that excellence of deed, all the worlds have been made your wife.

O Lord of Men, having crossed over the circular mountains whose ridges are girdled by rows of waters, you have—by means of the *cintāmaṇi* jewel—from within the interior of Badaradvīpa, fulfilled the expectations of your supplicants with its full fruit; from you, therefore, arise for the wise the sprouts of the jewels of the true Dharma. With blood flowing from the fissures of heads split open by sword-blades, [the ground was drenched] by the *rakṣasas* who steal the vital energy of those with bodies as dark as a dense canopy of clouds.

Because you allayed my hunger with your own flesh, which was not devoid of its natural heat, and because you severed the thirst for existence arising from birth through such yogic practices, by that merit may you attain liberation. Because King Śibi, being virtuous, offered his body—whose throat was parched and trembling from the terror of the hawk, and which lay upon his lap—to the bird so that it might find peace, he placed that body on a scale against one stained by the outpouring of blood; by that merit, Māra has reduced your body to the insignificance of a tuft of fine silk fluttering on a scale.

Because you cast aside even Lakṣmī—who grants desired fruits and never fails—and having made your lowest birth one that connects you to animal existence, you brought relief through your own flesh to those piercing pains; therefore, the powers of your intellects, which cut through the poison of afflictions, remain unimpeded.

That [body] which was like a mass of splendor, a fruit of the intense power of merits, tall and smeared with drops of blood, yet appearing dark blue like the luster of a shimmering water-lily—[by offering it, your powers remain unimpeded].
"Having plucked out his own two eyes, he gave them to a Brahmin who was sightless; therefore, you have become the sole lofty lamp for this world which is blind and shrouded in darkness.

Thus, O Jina, this [praise] has been shown by me through my own effort, adorned with the words of the sages; yet not even a fraction of the mass of your qualities has been mentioned. For, just as when drawing water from the ocean to fill a jar of stars, only a tiny drop of water is perceived at the edge of the shore, so too is my description of you.

Through this composition of even a mere fraction of a portion of the excellence of your conduct— which is the source of the accumulation of all that is auspicious for me, whose share is gathered through devotion blossoming from vast grace— may I become a person intent solely on the welfare of others among those who know all things, one who is devoted to the benefit of others and has little regard for his own self-interest.
— The *Jātakastava* by Ācārya Jñānayaśas.
